title: Care across the England–Wales border
label: 11 November 2026 · Cross-border healthcare
summary: The committee examined how Welsh patients are referred to English hospitals, who coordinates their care, and how differences in waiting arrangements, language support and computer systems affect patients. The witnesses said routine referrals usually work well, but acknowledged that long waits, split responsibilities and poor information-sharing can cause problems. They identified more consistent standards and better digital connections as priorities, while noting that many communication difficulties also occur within England.

glossary.definition: A service that checks referrals from Welsh GP practices and directs them to the appropriate English hospital service.
A request for funding for a particular patient's treatment when it is not routinely available through the usual arrangements.
Highly complex healthcare, often provided by only a small number of hospitals.
NHS organisations in England that plan and fund healthcare for their local populations.
Digital records that let different health and care services see some information about the same patient.
An NHS England service that allows authorised health staff to view some patient information.
A system that lets authorised services access information held in English general practice records.
A law that gives NHS England powers to require technology suppliers to follow certain data standards.
An NHS requirement to identify and meet patients' communication needs, such as providing information in a suitable format.
Short for integrated care board, an NHS organisation in England that plans and funds local healthcare.

chapters.title: How referrals reach English hospitals
chapters.takeaway: Most referrals follow a clear route, but very specialised treatments can involve extra approval steps.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How does a Welsh patient get referred to an English hospital, and where can the process become difficult?

turns.speaker: Simon Evans
turns.text: It usually starts with a GP, just as it would for an English patient. For Welsh patients going to an English hospital, the GP uses the Referral Assessment Service. The referral is checked and sent to the right hospital team, which reviews it and contacts the patient to arrange an appointment.

turns.speaker: Simon Evans
turns.text: The hospital then manages the patient's care through treatment and, ideally, a safe discharge. The referral itself is usually quick—often only a few days. How soon the patient is seen depends on the hospital's available appointments and waiting times.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So the time taken to pass on a referral is different from the time spent waiting for assessment and treatment.

turns.speaker: Simon Evans
turns.text: Yes. They are separate parts of the process.

turns.speaker: Henry Tufnell
turns.text: Welsh patients can be referred through different arrangements, including local health boards and national joint commissioning. Do English providers understand the different rules and does the route affect patients' experience?

turns.speaker: Roz Lindridge
turns.text: For specialised services, the rules and decision-making arrangements are clearly set out, and the Welsh and English teams work well together. The different referral figures may relate to different types of service, so I can't explain the numbers without checking them.

turns.speaker: Caroline Smith
turns.text: Some of the figures may also include people who live in England but have a Welsh-registered GP. Around 600 people a year are supported through the Referral Assessment Service in that way.

turns.speaker: Henry Tufnell
turns.text: I'm asking whether a patient gets a different experience depending on which organisation sends the referral.

turns.speaker: Caroline Smith
turns.text: In Gloucestershire, staff understand that different patients may follow different funding and approval processes. I don't think patients usually notice a difference in the referral itself.

turns.speaker: Simon Evans
turns.text: Most routine referrals go straight to the right service. The funding decision may come later, once the hospital understands what treatment is needed.

turns.speaker: Henry Tufnell
turns.text: We've heard that things work best when clinicians already know each other. If there's no established relationship and patients have to rely on the formal system, the process can feel unclear. Is that a problem?

turns.speaker: Roz Lindridge
turns.text: Relationships are well established for common services such as cancer and heart care. The challenge is more likely with very specialised services, where only a few hospitals provide the treatment and clinical teams may not already work together.

turns.speaker: Roz Lindridge
turns.text: We could make the route clearer for those services. We have learned from arrangements with Scotland, where there is a more formal agreement about which highly specialised services patients can access across the border. That might reduce unnecessary administration.

chapters.title: Care coordination and waiting times
chapters.takeaway: English hospitals coordinate care after accepting a referral, but split waiting arrangements and delays in communication can disrupt patients' journeys.

turns.speaker: Steve Witherden
turns.text: People in Powys often have to travel to Shropshire for hospital care. Once an English hospital accepts a Welsh patient, who is responsible for coordinating their care?

turns.speaker: Simon Evans
turns.text: The English hospital is responsible from accepting the referral through treatment and discharge. It may need to work with Welsh community or GP services, and that's where communication can become difficult.

turns.speaker: Steve Witherden
turns.text: Do clinicians have to rely on personal contacts because the two countries use different computer systems?

turns.speaker: Simon Evans
turns.text: Different hospitals have different levels of digital capability, and communication can be harder across the border. Hospitals should still send information to the referring clinician and provide discharge information to the patient, sometimes electronically and sometimes on paper.

turns.speaker: Henry Tufnell
turns.text: We've heard that patients can face broken-up pathways, slow communication and uncertainty about who is responsible. What do you do to make care feel joined up?

turns.speaker: Simon Evans
turns.text: The hospital should pass information on when a patient moves into community care. Delays in letters and records can cause problems, including within England. A single NHS service for patients would help, but the NHS app doesn't yet work smoothly across English and Welsh services.

turns.speaker: Roz Lindridge
turns.text: Our cross-border network brings together patient organisations and health service representatives. They can raise repeated problems and share lessons. There are also formal consultation processes when services are being changed.

turns.speaker: Caroline Smith
turns.text: In Gloucestershire, people who use the Referral Assessment Service give positive feedback about the referral process. That's feedback about getting into care, not about their treatment or how long they wait for an appointment.

turns.speaker: David Chadwick
turns.text: Powys has chosen to make some patients wait longer. At the same time, one-year waits at Wye Valley NHS Trust have risen by 75%, and waits over two years at Robert Jones and Agnes Hunt have risen by 370% since 2022. What does this mean for patients and hospitals?

turns.speaker: Simon Evans
turns.text: Those very long waits are for non-urgent treatment, not suspected cancer or some urgent diagnostic services. Welsh-funded and English-funded patients can be managed under different priorities, with the Welsh-funded capacity largely reserved for Welsh patients.

turns.speaker: Simon Evans
turns.text: That means some hospitals have to run two waiting arrangements, which their systems weren't designed for. It can be difficult for them to manage, though some hospitals with fewer Welsh patients don't keep a separate list.

turns.speaker: David Chadwick
turns.text: Could English hospitals treat patients sooner if the Welsh decision changed?

turns.speaker: Simon Evans
turns.text: They may be able to add capacity, but doing so quickly can cost more. Hospitals might need to buy extra services or use private providers.

turns.speaker: Roz Lindridge
turns.text: Hospitals are also working to improve how much they can do with the resources they have. Clinicians have warned that long waits can worsen a patient's condition and mean they need more treatment later.

turns.speaker: David Chadwick
turns.text: What is the relationship like with Powys, given its plans to change community hospitals and services?

turns.speaker: Roz Lindridge
turns.text: The proposals are being consulted on. Powys is due to discuss them at the cross-border network, where English health organisations can give their views.

turns.speaker: Simon Evans
turns.text: Different approaches by Welsh and English commissioners can make things more difficult for hospitals and put pressure on their working relationships.

turns.speaker: Steve Witherden
turns.text: Do patients understand why people at the same hospital may have different waiting rules and treatment options?

turns.speaker: Caroline Smith
turns.text: I can't speak for Shropshire. In Gloucestershire, the hospital doesn't keep separate waiting lists for Welsh and English patients. We have a strong relationship with Aneurin Bevan Health Board and involve it when we consult on service changes that may affect people over the border.

turns.speaker: Caroline Smith
turns.text: We have about 9,000 Gloucestershire residents registered with Welsh GP practices. They should have a voice in service planning even though they are a small part of our population.

turns.speaker: Steve Witherden
turns.text: Do you hear from Welsh patients about whether access is fair and consistent?

turns.speaker: Caroline Smith
turns.text: Not in a way I can report on locally. Patients can give feedback through the same hospital surveys as anyone else.

turns.speaker: Roz Lindridge
turns.text: The patient group Llais has also reviewed rural healthcare and shared its findings with the cross-border network. Healthwatch representatives can raise concerns there too.

chapters.title: Welsh-language support
chapters.takeaway: Interpretation is available in Gloucestershire, but witnesses said language needs must be identified early and consistent expectations matter.

turns.speaker: Ann Davies
turns.text: How do hospitals support Welsh-speaking patients, especially children from Welsh-speaking families and older people who may feel more comfortable using Welsh?

turns.speaker: Caroline Smith
turns.text: In Gloucestershire, patients can use interpretation services in hospitals and community services. Welsh interpretation can be arranged face to face, by video or by phone. Urgent calls can use an on-demand service; for important or complex discussions, staff can arrange an interpreter in person.

turns.speaker: Simon Evans
turns.text: Hospitals use the same general approach for Welsh as for other languages. Face-to-face interpretation is particularly important for vulnerable patients and when staff need to discuss serious matters.

turns.speaker: Ann Davies
turns.text: How do you make sure the hospital knows a patient needs an interpreter before the appointment?

turns.speaker: Caroline Smith
turns.text: Ideally, the GP records that need and it is passed on when the hospital books the appointment. It doesn't always happen. Patients are also told how to contact the hospital about language or other communication needs.

turns.speaker: Ann Davies
turns.text: Can information and letters be provided in Welsh, as well as in other languages?

turns.speaker: Caroline Smith
turns.text: Yes. The Accessible Information Standard requires staff to discuss patients' communication needs and make suitable arrangements. In practice, it also informs how services respond to language needs.

turns.speaker: Caroline Smith
turns.text: If an interpreter hasn't been booked, the telephone service can connect staff to one quickly—usually in about a minute and a half. That isn't always as good as meeting an interpreter in person, but it means the conversation can happen.

turns.speaker: Ann Davies
turns.text: Should Welsh-language expectations be made clearer in contracts and cross-border agreements?

turns.speaker: Roz Lindridge
turns.text: Clear standards should apply across services. I don't have evidence of a widespread problem, but expectations need to be understood in hospitals, GP practices and community care.

turns.speaker: Roz Lindridge
turns.text: If we asked for more extensive language services, we would need to consider the costs, staffing and training required, and how the changes would benefit patients.

chapters.title: Sharing records and using NHS apps
chapters.takeaway: Some information can cross the border, but many records remain in separate systems and a complete, easy-to-use service is still a long way off.

turns.speaker: David Chadwick
turns.text: Families have told us that when someone is discharged from an English hospital to receive care in Wales, their information sometimes doesn't follow them. What is being done to improve cross-border sharing?

turns.speaker: Ian Townend
turns.text: There isn't one place where all a patient's health information is held. GP practices, hospitals and community and mental health services keep separate records, often on different computer systems. Even a large hospital trust may use more than 200 systems.

turns.speaker: Ian Townend
turns.text: This is a problem within England as well as across the border. England has made progress with the National Care Records Service and shared records, but hospitals still can't easily share all their information with other services.

turns.speaker: Ian Townend
turns.text: Information also has to be recorded in ways that different systems can understand. We need common rules for how messages, medical terms and codes are used, as well as clear rules about who is allowed to see records.

turns.speaker: Ian Townend
turns.text: We work with Digital Health and Care Wales on this. Digital leaders from the four UK nations and Ireland now meet quarterly, and working groups are developing shared standards, especially between England and Wales.

turns.speaker: Ian Townend
turns.text: The standards are being developed together, but each country decides how to adopt them. A new English law also gives NHS England powers to require technology suppliers to follow standards. We're discussing with Wales how that power could help both countries.

turns.speaker: Ian Townend
turns.text: Some local systems already let services on the other side of the border see some information. For example, some Welsh services can access English shared records, and some English services can use the National Care Records Service to see limited information from Welsh areas.

turns.speaker: David Chadwick
turns.text: What are the specific obstacles, and what needs to happen next?

turns.speaker: Ian Townend
turns.text: GP information is easier to access. English GP practices use three main suppliers, while Wales has moved to one supplier. Hospitals use many more systems, and some suppliers have been reluctant to make their information available.

turns.speaker: Ian Townend
turns.text: The technical standards exist, but services still need to put them into practice. There are also questions about permissions and how staff prove their identity when they access records.

turns.speaker: Ian Townend
turns.text: The next step is for national digital leaders to agree shared priorities and make sure the teams underneath them work on those priorities.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We were discussing these problems ten years ago. Are quarterly meetings really going to make a difference when information still doesn't reliably follow patients?

turns.speaker: Ian Townend
turns.text: Some local systems already provide access, and more information is becoming available through national services. But hospitals still can't easily share records outside their own organisations, even within England. There's now more pressure to solve that, including through work on a single patient record.

turns.speaker: Andrew Ranger
turns.text: Can Welsh patients use digital services across the border for appointments, records and prescriptions? And can the NHS Wales app be used in Welsh?

turns.speaker: Ian Townend
turns.text: There are two apps, and which one a person can use depends on where their GP is, not where they live or receive care. People can register for either the NHS app or the NHS Wales app, but not both.

turns.speaker: Ian Townend
turns.text: The apps share some technology, but the information they show is limited. In England, people can see GP information and some details about medicines, appointments, referrals and test results. They can't yet see their full hospital record or discharge summary.

turns.speaker: Ian Townend
turns.text: There may be a way for future services, including a single patient record, to make information available through either app. But I don't know of specific work underway to make cross-border services such as ordering prescriptions available.

turns.speaker: Ian Townend
turns.text: There is progress on Welsh-language access. NHS login, which verifies someone's identity, is currently only in English. A trial has shown how it could work in Welsh, and NHS Wales is discussing whether to commission it as a live service.

chapters.title: Reforms and priorities for improvement
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses expect local relationships to continue through English NHS restructuring, but want more consistent rules and better digital links.

turns.speaker: Gerald Jones
turns.text: England is changing how its health organisations are arranged. Could larger integrated care boards and the planned changes to NHS England make it harder to keep Welsh patients a priority?

turns.speaker: Roz Lindridge
turns.text: The proposed law is still being considered, so I don't want to assume what it will do. English integrated care boards have already been reduced and combined, but local planning and relationships still happen at neighbourhood and community level.

turns.speaker: Roz Lindridge
turns.text: The boards and their new groupings have considered cross-border patients. The Department of Health and NHS England have also said that agreements with Wales and other devolved nations should continue.

turns.speaker: Roz Lindridge
turns.text: Many day-to-day links are between hospitals, GP practices and community services, and those relationships should continue through structural changes. The cross-border network and existing planning and emergency arrangements also provide continuity.

turns.speaker: Caroline Smith
turns.text: In Gloucestershire, we work in a group with Bristol, North Somerset and South Gloucestershire, but keep local neighbourhood arrangements. One neighbourhood covers the border area, where voluntary organisations already work across county boundaries.

turns.speaker: Gerald Jones
turns.text: Are local relationships enough to ensure Welsh patients aren't overlooked by larger English organisations?

turns.speaker: Roz Lindridge
turns.text: National policy and the shared statement of principles will continue to set expectations. The regional NHS team can also check whether English hospitals and boards are meeting their responsibilities and step in to support discussions if needed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If you could make one change to improve cross-border care, what would it be?

turns.speaker: Roz Lindridge
turns.text: Make the standards requested by the English and Welsh governments more consistent, so patients have fairer access and services can meet the expectations in practice.

turns.speaker: Simon Evans
turns.text: Make the waiting-time systems more consistent between England and Wales.

turns.speaker: Caroline Smith
turns.text: Improve the digital connections between our systems, particularly for the clinicians making referrals.

turns.speaker: Ian Townend
turns.text: Make patient information and services accessible regardless of which system created them or which side of the border they're on.
